newsitem.title: CONGO: France starts military pullout from Congo.
newsitem.headline: France starts military pullout from Congo.

text.p: France began withdrawing its military force from the Congo Republic capital on Monday after evacuating more than 5,000 foreign nationals caught in a bloody political and ethnic dispute in its former colony.

With the diplomatic focus shifting to peace talks hosted by neighbour and fellow oil-producer Gabon, Brazzaville enjoyed a relative lull in fighting -- despite the occasional burst of shooting which has been part of life in the city since June 5.

France is pressing ahead with the withdrawal despite an appeal from Congo President Pascal Lissouba that it leave troops in the city as a buffer force between the army and militiamen loyal to former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

"We have already started taking out less essential equipment and in the afternoon the first troops will leave. They are already packing their bags," French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pellissier, told reporters on Monday.

France had around 1,200 soldiers in the city. They initially went as part of a Western operation to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa, in the event of a bloodbath at the end of the civil war in former Zaire. It never occurred.

"About 300 (soldiers) are expected to leave today for Chad and Gabon on 16 flights. Combat units will stay until the last moment to show a presence and to ensure security at the airport," Pelissier said.

Reception points in the city for evacuees who were kept there before being brought to the airport have been closed. An estimated 30 foreigners who did not make it on Sunday were to be flown out on Monday on military flights.
"If somebody calls to us for help, then we will still pull them out even up to the last minute," the spokesman said.
Sporadic firing of mortars, rocket-propelled grenades and machineguns could be heard around the airport through the night, but it was quiet compared to the night before.
"It appears relatively calm at the airport today and I believe it is the same in town," the French spokesman said.

France is keeping its embassy open. "We have not contemplated closing our embassy but naturally we will take the necessary measures to ensure its protection," a Foreign Ministry spokesman in Paris said. He could not say how many soldiers would stay on to guard the embassy.
The conflict began when the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home in a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a presidential election scheduled for July 27.
The death toll from the fighting could run into hundreds, or even thousands according to some sources.
The two rivals declared a truce on Wednesday.

After a two-day lull, fighting flared on Sunday. Government loyalists rained shells down on positions held by Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militiamen from the hills behind the city's airport. The militia fired mortars and tank shells.
Some Western analysts fear the battle will be stepped up around the airport once the French leave.

Envoys of Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso left on the same plane on Sunday for talks in Gabon's capital Libreville. "If we did not believe negotiations would work, we wouldn't be going," Lissouba representative Marius Mounbenday said.
Lissouba says the election should take place as planned. Sassou Nguesso has called for guarantees of transparency, fairness and security first.
Lissouba has also called for an African peace force. Mediators say this will be on the agenda of the Gabon talks.
